questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Hearing a melodic interval and the two lines that give it
questions.learningObjective: name the two melodies that could produce a heard melodic interval
questions.explanation: A melodic interval is measured between two notes that sound one after the other, so a line qualifies only if the two notes are adjacent with nothing between them. In the line that leaps straight from the lower note to the upper one, the leap itself is the interval, and a listener can match it by singing the same leap. The other line fills the gap with the intervening pitches, so the rising motion is a chain of seconds and the leap never sounds at all. The trap is to pick the line that reaches the same top note, which confuses arriving at a pitch with hearing an interval. The two melodies are distinguished by what happens between the notes, not by where the line ends.
questions.hint: Check which line moves from the lower note to the upper note in one step, with no intermediate note.

options.text: The line that leaps straight from C4 to G4 with nothing in between, because the leap itself sounds the interval
The line that climbs C4, D4, E4, F4, G4 in seconds, because a run of steps also contains the interval
options.misconception: believes filling the gap with intermediate notes still exposes the leap to the ear

options.text: The line that arrives at G4 after a descent and a turn, because the arrival point fixes the interval
options.misconception: confuses ending on a pitch with hearing the step that reached it

options.text: Either line will do, since a listener matches the interval and ignores the notes that lead into it
options.misconception: assumes the approach notes are irrelevant to hearing an interval sung as a leap

The trap is to answer 4, which is the size of the first leap alone, or 3, which is the second.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a harmonic interval adds to a melodic one
questions.learningObjective: explain how sounding the notes together changes what the listener hears
questions.explanation: When two notes sound together the ear compares them at a single instant, so the interval is heard as one fused colour with a definite brightness or tension, and the lower note is heard as a bass supporting the upper. Sung in sequence the same two pitches are heard as a gesture, a move from one place to another, and the memory of the first note is what supplies the comparison. That is why a harmonic interval can be named by ear in isolation while a melodic interval depends on the line around it. The trap is to think the two are interchangeable, which would make the same interval sound equally fused in a melody and in a chord.
questions.hint: Ask what the ear can do with two pitches at once that it cannot do with one pitch after the other.

It changes the interval's name, so the same two notes form a different quality when sounded together

options.text: It adds nothing, since an interval is defined only by the two pitches and never by how they are placed in time
options.misconception: treats placement in time as irrelevant to what the listener hears

options.text: It makes the lower note disappear, so a harmonic interval is heard as the upper note standing on its own

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What an inversion does to an interval's number and quality
questions.learningObjective: state how inverting an interval alters its number and its quality
questions.explanation: Moving the bass up an octave turns a second into a seventh and a fifth into a fourth, so the two numbers always add to nine, which is why a fourth inverts to a fifth and a third inverts to a sixth. The quality rule is that perfect intervals stay perfect and imperfect ones swap between major and minor, with augmented and diminished exchanging places. A perfect fifth therefore inverts to a perfect fourth rather than to a diminished one, which is what makes a fifth so stable. The trap is to assume the quality is left untouched, which would turn a major sixth into a perfect third instead of a minor third.

options.text: Both the number and the quality change together, so a perfect fifth inverts to an imperfect fourth
options.misconception: claims a perfect fifth inverts to a diminished or major fourth

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why inversion alters the number but keeps the colour
questions.learningObjective: explain what inverting an interval changes and what it preserves
questions.explanation: The number is forced by the octave. Moving the lower note up an octave reverses which note is further from the starting point, and since an octave holds seven letter names, a number of n always inverts to a number of 9 minus n. That is arithmetic, not taste, which is why a fourth and a fifth are the two halves of one relationship. The quality is a separate judgement about how the semitones are distributed inside that number, and inverting the pair leaves the distribution intact for perfect intervals while swapping major for minor, because a major sixth and a minor third are the same two pitches read in the opposite direction. The trap is to reason that a bigger number should be a bigger sound; consonance follows the quality and the number together, not the number alone.
questions.hint: Ask how many letter names fit into an octave, and then ask which intervals sound stable in any position.

answer.exemplar: Two separate things are happening, and separating them is the whole answer. The number is arithmetic forced by the octave: an octave holds seven letter names, and once the lower note is lifted the count runs the other way, so n inverts to 9 minus n. A fourth inverts to a fifth and a fifth to a fourth, a second to a seventh and a seventh to a second, and a third to a sixth and a sixth to a third, every time. That is why the two numbers of an inversion always add to nine. The quality is a different judgement, because it asks how the semitones are spread inside that number rather than how many names are counted. Inversion leaves that distribution alone for perfect intervals, so a perfect fifth becomes a perfect fourth and stays consonant, and it exchanges major with minor for imperfect intervals, so a major sixth of 9 semitones becomes a minor third of 3. The mistake to avoid is carrying consonance over from the number, so that a sixth is assumed to sound wider and more open than a third. The reason that is wrong is that the same two pitches can be read in either direction, and the ear hears the pair, not the direction of the count.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why a tritone resolves differently from a fourth
questions.learningObjective: explain the different resolutions of a tritone and a perfect fourth
questions.explanation: A tritone is a fourth built on the leading tone, so its upper note is a half step below the tonic and its lower note a half step above the tonic, and both notes are therefore pulled outward toward the tonic. Moving outward stretches the pair from six semitones to a sixth, which is consonant, and the bass note of the chord above it takes the tritone's place. A perfect fourth is not a dissonance in the same way: it is the interval of a subdominant function, so the note that resolves is the upper one, falling by step to a third above a stationary bass, which closes a chord. The trap is to treat both as the same kind of tension, when one is a pair of simultaneous leading tones and the other is a single note waiting over a bass.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two notes in each interval carries the pull toward the key's fifth degree.

options.text: A tritone is a fourth built on the leading tone, so both of its notes are pulled outward while a fourth resolves in one note against a bass

options.text: A fourth resolves outward because it is the interval of the dominant, while a tritone resolves inward because it is the interval of the tonic
options.misconception: assigns the fourth to dominant and the tritone to tonic, which reverses their functions

options.text: Neither interval resolves by step; both are left standing and the surrounding chords change around them instead
options.misconception: believes dissonant intervals are simply abandoned in place rather than resolved by step

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why the perfect fifth is a stable interval
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes the perfect fifth stable in inversion and in tuning
questions.explanation: Two features together account for it. First, a perfect fifth is the only interval besides the octave whose inversion is another perfect interval, so it never turns harsh when the bass moves and a composer can place it freely in any voice without a change of colour. Second, the two pitches stand in the simplest ratio after one to one, three to two, so the fifth is the first interval the ear recognises as a ratio at all and it is the first partial that the overtone series produces after the octave. The trap is to attribute the stability to loudness or to position in a chord, neither of which travels with the interval when it moves.
questions.hint: Ask what the perfect fifth becomes when the two notes are exchanged, and what the simple ratio of the two pitches is.

options.text: Its inversion is another perfect interval and its two pitches stand in the simplest ratio, so it survives any change of bass
It is the widest interval a singer can produce, so its size itself is what the ear finds restful
options.misconception: believes the fifth is consonant because it is wide, which would rank the minor seventh as well

options.text: It is the interval a tonic triad and a dominant triad share, so chords built on it agree with each other
options.misconception: confuses a property of the interval with a coincidence between two chord roots

options.text: It keeps the same size at any register, so a fifth sung low and one sung high are identical in every respect
options.misconception: treats octave equivalence of size as if it settled the whole question of consonance

questions.topic: Telling a major sixth from a minor sixth by ear
questions.learningObjective: state what separates a major sixth from a minor sixth in a sung pair
questions.explanation: The two differ by a single semitone and nothing else, so the ear is deciding between 9 semitones and 8 semitones, and a singer learns the difference as how much space the pair leaves. The same relationship holds under inversion, since a major sixth inverted is a minor third and a minor sixth inverted is a major third, so a sixth is judged against the thirds it can be turned into. The trap is to expect a change of letter name between the two, when both span six names and only the inner spacing differs. Another trap is to assume the wider one is always the brighter, since a major third is also wider than a minor third yet the ear ranks them in the opposite order.

options.text: The dynamic level, so a louder sixth is a major sixth and a softer sixth is a minor sixth

questions.topic: Why a diminished seventh chord is ambiguous
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a diminished seventh chord usable in several keys
questions.explanation: Stacking three equal minor thirds divides the octave into four equal parts, so the four notes of the chord sit a diminished seventh apart and any one of them can serve as the leading tone of a different key. A singer hearing B, D, F, A flat against a C in the bass reads the chord as leading to C, while the identical sounding chord against a D sharp in the bass is heard as leading to D sharp. Because the divisions are equal, no note of the chord is acoustically privileged, which is what allows the reinterpretation. The trap is to think the chord is somehow vague because it is unstable; it is not vague, it is a dominant-function chord whose resolution is simply not fixed until the bass arrives.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the chord's four notes when the ear supplies a different tonic.

options.text: Three equal minor thirds divide the octave evenly, so any one of the four notes can be heard as the leading tone of a different key

options.text: The chord is missing a third, so it can be completed upward into whichever triad the key happens to require

questions.topic: The tendency tones inside an augmented sixth chord
questions.learningObjective: identify the two tendency tones of an augmented sixth chord
questions.explanation: The augmented sixth chord exists to be widened out of the way and then closed, and the two notes that do the work are A flat, the lowered sixth degree, and F sharp, the raised fourth degree. Both sit a half step from the fifth degree, G, and they must move in opposite directions to get there: A flat descends a whole step to G and F sharp ascends a half step to G. The C in the middle is a common tone and does not resolve. The trap is to treat the F sharp as a raised leading tone heading to G sharp, which would aim the chord at a different key, or to send A flat upward instead of downward, which would spoil the widening the chord exists to achieve.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The function of a cadential six four
questions.learningObjective: explain why a six four chord on a dominant bass is a dominant chord
questions.explanation: The bass note decides. A G in the bass is the fifth degree of C major, so anything built on it is in the dominant family, and a six four over that bass is a dominant chord with the tonic triad's notes piled on top of it as decoration. It arrives on a weak part of the bar, it delays the dominant, and it is followed by the dominant itself, which is the definition of a cadential six four. The trap is to read the figured bass alone, where a six four over a tonic bass is genuinely pre-dominant, and to assume the numeral describes the chord above the bass rather than the function of the bass note beneath it.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why contrary motion between outer voices sounds independent
questions.learningObjective: explain what contrary motion contributes that similar motion does not
questions.explanation: The interval between the voices is what the ear follows as well as the notes, and in contrary motion the two lines do not reinforce a single contour. The soprano's descent is heard against the bass's ascent, so each line supplies a direction the other lacks and neither can be predicted from the other. In similar motion the outer voices move as one, and when they move in parallel they also hold the same interval, so the pair reads as a single line doubled rather than as two. The trap is to think independence comes from the register of the two lines, when it comes from the relationship between their directions.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the distance between the voices when they move together and when they move apart.

answer.exemplar: What the ear follows in two voices is not only the two pitches but the interval between them, and contrary motion is defined by what happens to that interval. When the soprano descends as the bass ascends, the two lines pull in opposite directions, so the distance between them changes constantly and neither line can be inferred from the other. Each voice is therefore heard as carrying information the other does not, which is exactly the impression of independent composition. In similar motion both lines travel the same way, so one contour governs both and the pair is heard as a single gesture. In parallel motion the two also hold the same interval throughout, so the doubling is heard in the interval as much as in the notes, which is why parallel fifths and octaves are faulted even though the ear finds the pair smooth. The wrong belief to avoid is that independence is a matter of register, so that a soprano and a bass in different octaves sound independent whenever they are widely spaced. Wide spacing alone gives no such result: two lines an octave and a sixth apart moving in parallel fifths are heard as a single doubled line, because the parallel motion is the stronger cue.

questions.learningObjective: state what the harmonic minor scale alters and when the alteration applies

The trap is to think the raised seventh is a decorative inflection applied only on the way up.

questions.explanation: The three minor thirds of the chord divide the octave into four equal parts, so the four notes are a diminished seventh apart from one another and none of them is acoustically distinguished. That is why the same four pitches can be read as a leading-tone chord in four different keys, and why a single accidental change in the bass is enough to redirect the whole chord. The second half of the answer is that the chord is genuinely ambiguous only while the bass withholds the answer: the moment a bass note arrives, the ear picks the reading in which the chord's root is a half step above it, and the resolution becomes unambiguous.
questions.hint: Ask how the four notes of the chord are spaced, and then ask which note tells the ear where it is going.

answer.exemplar: The chord is built from three stacked minor thirds, and three minor thirds divide the octave into four equal parts, so its four notes sit a diminished seventh apart and the spacing between them is uniform. Nothing in the chord itself says which of the four notes is the root, because no note is more prominent than any other, so the chord can be read as a leading-tone seventh in any of four keys without altering a single written note. In C major the reading is B, D, F and A flat resolving up to C; the same four pitches respelled resolve to E major from the same sounding chord. The second condition is the bass. The chord stays ambiguous only for as long as the bass withholds the answer, because it is the bass note that tells the ear which of the four notes is being treated as the root, and the ear picks the reading in which that bass lies a half step below the root it assumes. Once the bass arrives, the reading is settled and the resolution that follows is no longer a choice. The wrong belief to avoid is that a chord is either ambiguous or not regardless of what is underneath it. The ambiguity belongs to the chord in combination with its bass, so a single bass note change is enough to move the music into a new key while every upper voice stays exactly where it was.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a secondary dominant tonicises a degree
questions.learningObjective: identify the key a secondary dominant tonicises and the note that reveals it
questions.explanation: The chord is a secondary dominant, a major triad built a fifth above the G chord so that G is momentarily treated as a tonic of its own. The note that gives it away is F sharp, because the triad C major would build on D is a minor one containing F natural, and the raised third is what turns it into a dominant. The chord therefore tonicises the dominant and then hands the music back to the key, which is what makes it a brief local departure rather than a modulation. The trap is to hear any major triad that includes an accidental as a modulation, when the test is where it goes next and whether the key it implies is diatonic.
questions.hint: Ask which chord would normally appear in C major on D, and which note the major triad needs that C major does not supply.

options.text: It is the dominant of the submediant, so the F sharp tonicises the A minor chord rather than the G chord
options.misconception: identifies the tonicised chord from the accidental rather than from where the chord goes

The raised third is the whole point of the chord, because a major third above the root is what makes a triad a dominant rather than the minor triad the key would otherwise supply on that degree. The trap is 3, the size of the minor third that C major's own triad on D would contain.

questions.topic: Reading the chords above a repeating ground bass
questions.learningObjective: decide which chord does not belong above a stated ground bass
questions.explanation: The ground fixes the key as D minor, and the chords that belong over it are the tonic, the subdominant, the dominant and the chords borrowed from D major, which is D minor's parallel. D minor, B flat major and G minor are all diatonic, and A major is the borrowed chord from the parallel major that supplies a major dominant. What does not belong is nothing on the list except, if it had appeared, a triad whose root lay outside both D minor and D major. The trap is to name B flat major as foreign, because its root is a whole tone from the tonic, when in fact it is the subdominant of D minor and one of the three chords the ground is designed to carry.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: An ostinato and its harmonic effect
questions.learningObjective: state what an ostinato is and what it does not determine harmonically
questions.explanation: The pattern is an ostinato, and its defining property is that it repeats without variation, which fixes a rhythmic and melodic frame below the music. What it does not do is name the key or the harmony: the same ostinato can sit over a different set of chords in each statement, and the ear is left to hear the changes above it as a harmonic argument. That is the effect, a constant against which variety is heard sharply. The trap is to treat the ostinato as a bass line that determines the harmony, which confuses it with a ground, where the repeating material is specifically in the bass and the chords above it are what vary.
questions.hint: Ask what the pattern fixes and what remains free above it.

options.text: A sequence, which fixes the harmony because each statement of the pattern implies the chord beneath it

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that counts ostinato statements

questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that produces a retrograde and reports the interval it spans
questions.explanation: Reading the list backwards gives G4, F4, E4, D4, C4, so the retrograde runs the original line in reverse and the effect is rhythmic rather than harmonic: the line's own durations now sit under a contour that fights them, so the accents land against the phrasing. Counting downward from G to C spans 7 semitones, since the ladder from G down passes G sharp, A, A sharp, B, C. The second route subtracts the pitch classes and reduces, with C as 0 and G as 7, which gives 7, and the downward count is the same 7 because the reversed line runs from the higher note to the lower one. The trap is 5, which is the distance the other way round, from C up to G, and the rule's word downward is what rules it out.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that places a canon's entries

questions.explanation: The tie makes position 4 into the sounding attack, because a tied note is struck once at the start of the tie and not again, so the note beginning on position 4 runs through position 5 and into position 6. The metrical grid makes position 1 the strongest position and position 4 the weakest, so an attack on position 4 displaces the accent onto the weak part of the bar, which is the definition of a syncopation. The second route is the same fact read as arithmetic: the grid has 6 positions, the second beat occupies positions 3 and 4, and the attack lands on the second of those two. questions.explanation: A bar of 6/8 holds 6 eighth notes written as two groups of three, so it holds 12 eighth notes in total, and the three quarter notes are read as three equal groups, so 12 divided by 3 is 4 eighth notes each. The second route measures in quarter notes: 6/8 holds the equivalent of three quarters, and three quarters spread over three groups is exactly one quarter per group, which is 4 eighth notes. The reason it sounds like a jolt is that the ear is given three beats where the metre promises two, while the total duration stays the same. The trap is 3, which is the length of one of the metre's own groups and not the length of a note in the hemiola's regrouping.

questions.topic: Finding a cadential point against a metrical grid

questions.explanation: The final chord is E major, and in a key of A major the chord on E is the dominant, not the tonic, so the piece cannot be closing in A major when it stops on the dominant. A piece whose final chord is the dominant of its own key has not resolved, which is the mark of a piece that ends abruptly, or of one whose actual key is E. questions.topic: Testing a claim about function against a resolution
questions.learningObjective: explain how a resolution tests a stated claim about tonal function
questions.explanation: The resolution is the evidence, and it works on the key claim before it works on the function claim. The passage ends on C major, and a piece or section that closes on C has arrived at C, so the key is C major and not F major; the same reasoning applied to the opening chord would give the same answer, and the ending is the stronger witness because a close is where a tonal centre is stated most plainly. With the key settled, the D minor chord is a supertonic in C major, so the second half of the claim fails too. The trap is to accept the key from the first chord, which is often right but is not what a resolution is evidence of.
questions.hint: Ask which chord the claim makes the goal of the passage, and then look at where the passage actually stops.

answer.exemplar: A resolution is the test, because it shows where the harmony has been travelling. The passage ends on C major, and an ending is the strongest single piece of evidence a passage offers about its tonal centre, since a close states the centre more plainly than an opening does. So the key claim fails first: a passage that ends on C major is in C major, and a reading of F major would require the music to come to rest on F or on C as the dominant of F, which is a different argument from the one the writer has made. Only after the key is settled can the function claim be tested, and then it fails as well: with C as the tonic, the chord on D is the second degree, so D minor is a supertonic triad and not a subdominant. The wrong belief to avoid is that the first chord names the key, which is often true by accident and is not what a resolution is evidence of. A second wrong belief is that a chord's function can be asserted independently of the key, so that a triad on D might be called a subdominant in one reading and a supertonic in another. It can, but only across genuinely different readings, and here the ending has already fixed the reading.
